briefings.title: The rules in full
briefings.headline: Two rules and a cap. Miss them and the OBR says so on Budget day.

paragraphs.text: Your Budget is on Wednesday 28 October 2026. The Office for Budget Responsibility publishes a new forecast alongside it and, once a year at the autumn Budget, formally judges whether the Government's plans meet the fiscal rules. That judgement is the test your Budget has to pass.

The stability rule: by 2029-30, day-to-day spending must be paid for out of revenue. From this Budget, when 2029-30 becomes the third year of the forecast, a deficit of up to 0.5% of GDP is allowed. The investment rule: net financial liabilities, the rules' measure of debt, must be falling as a share of GDP in the same year. The welfare cap: most working-age and child benefits must stay within £194.5 billion plus a 5% margin.

Headroom is the margin by which you pass. March left £23.6 billion against the stability rule. Set against that, the OBR's typical five-year forecast error for receipts is 0.9% of GDP, about £33 billion: the forecast can move by more than the whole margin, which is why a Chancellor keeps some in hand.

briefings.title: What has moved since March
briefings.headline: Rates and inflation are above what the OBR assumed in March. Borrowing is running ahead of its path.

paragraphs.text: The OBR fixed its March assumptions in January: market interest rates from the ten working days to 22 January, and its own view of growth and inflation. The 10-year gilt yield it assumed was 4.5%; it is now about 5.35%. On the OBR's own reckoner a sustained 1 percentage point on rates adds about £15 billion to borrowing by 2030-31.

sources.quote: A sustained 1 percentage point increase in Bank Rate and gilt yields would increase borrowing by £15 billion in 2030-31

paragraphs.text: Independent forecasters expect more inflation and more borrowing than the OBR did: CPI of 3.1% this year against the OBR's 2.3%, and borrowing £27 billion above the OBR's path in 2029-30. None of this is a forecast of mine. The next step asks whose figures you will plan on; the OBR will publish its own in October whatever you choose.

briefings.title: The politics in full
briefings.headline: A new Prime Minister wants a Budget people notice. The manifesto says what you may not touch.

paragraphs.text: The Prime Minister took office in July and has moved fast: VAT off electricity bills from 1 October, bus fares capped at £2 for 2027, and a promise to put "life's essentials back under stronger public control". Downing Street wants this Budget to show the same energy, and will tell you what it is for.

sources.quote: put life's essentials back under stronger public control

paragraphs.text: The manifesto ties your hands: no rise in income tax rates, National Insurance or VAT, and corporation tax capped at 25% for the whole Parliament. Budget 2025 ended the two-child limit and repeated the tax lock. These are red lines, not preferences. Each lever will warn you before you cross one, and the public will notice if you do.

briefings.title: Where the money comes from
briefings.headline: Income tax, National Insurance and VAT raise 58% of everything.

paragraphs.text: Public sector receipts total £1,235bn in 2025-26. Income tax (£331bn), National Insurance (£204bn) and VAT (£181bn) raise 58% of it between them. Corporation tax adds £98.8bn, council tax £50.9bn, business rates £33.7bn, fuel duty £24.2bn, capital gains tax £21.8bn, property transaction taxes £16.9bn, alcohol and tobacco duties £20.0bn and inheritance tax £8.7bn.

Receipts are forecast to rise from 38.8% of GDP in 2024-25 to 42.7% in 2030-31. Within that, National Accounts taxes rise from 34.5% to 38.5% of GDP, which the OBR describes as a historic high and 5.6 percentage points above the pre-pandemic level of 32.9% in 2019-20.

Most of the rise comes from income tax and National Insurance (2.4 points of GDP), driven by earnings growth combined with the freeze in personal tax thresholds until April 2031, and from capital taxes (0.9 points), driven by rising equity prices and the October 2024 changes to inheritance tax and capital gains tax.

Treat the tax forecast as uncertain: the OBR's average absolute error in receipts as a share of GDP five years out is 0.9 percentage points. Yield from frozen thresholds is paid by a broad base and is less sensitive to behaviour, but highly sensitive to inflation.

briefings.title: What will be contested
briefings.headline: The threshold freeze raises the most and everyone pays it. Fuel duty has not risen since 2011.

paragraphs.text: The threshold freeze is the biggest revenue raiser in the system and is paid by everyone in work: the OBR notes its yield comes from a broad base of taxpayers. Ending it costs money in every year to 2031; extending it further is not on offer, because Budget 2025 already runs it to April 2031.

Fuel duty rates have not been increased since 2011-12 despite successive commitments to raise them; Budget 2025 planned staged rises from September 2026 and RPI uprating from April 2027. The OBR says holding the rate flat instead would cost about £3.6 billion a year from 2027-28.

VAT's zero and reduced rates are the largest reliefs in the tax system: HMRC costs the zero rate on food at £27.4bn in 2025-26, new dwellings at £14.6bn and the 5% rate on domestic fuel and power at £7.0bn. They are also the ones no Chancellor has touched since 2011.
The inheritance tax nil-rate band has been £325,000 since April 2009 and is frozen to April 2031, so more estates are drawn in each year; the 40% rate itself is the visible target.

briefings.title: Your predecessor's decisions
briefings.headline: Your predecessor raised £13bn from frozen thresholds alone. You can undo any of it.

paragraphs.text: Budget 2025 (26 November 2025) raised revenue mainly by extending the personal tax threshold freeze for three more years to April 2031 (£8.4bn in 2029-30 including the employer threshold), raising the rates on dividend, savings and property income (£2.2bn), capping salary-sacrifice pension contributions (£4.8bn) and raising remote gaming duty (£1.1bn), while cancelling fuel duty uprating for 2026-27 and extending the 5p cut to August 2026 (£-0.8bn). Each can be reversed here at the Treasury's own costing.

briefings.title: Income tax: rates that have not moved, thresholds that have not either
briefings.headline: Rates have barely moved since 2008. Frozen thresholds do the work instead.

paragraphs.text: The basic rate has been 20% since 2008-09, when it was cut from 22%; the higher rate has been 40% throughout; the additional rate has been 45% since 2013-14, after a year at 50%.

The personal allowance (£12,570) and the basic rate limit (£37,700, so a higher-rate threshold of £50,270) have been fixed in law since 2022-23 and, after Budget 2025, stay fixed until 2030-31, with indexation switched off.

Because earnings grow while thresholds stand still, more income is taxed and more of it at higher rates. The OBR attributes most of the rise in personal taxes to earnings growth combined with the freeze; income tax raises £331bn in 2025-26 and £414bn in 2029-30.
HMRC's ready reckoner costs a penny on the basic rate at about £8 billion a year; allowances and thresholds do not scale in a straight line, so those levers use HMRC's published points only.
A cap on the pension tax-free lump sum is reported again for this Budget. No costing has been published, so it is not on this desk.

briefings.title: National Insurance: cut for employees, raised for employers
briefings.headline: Cut for employees in 2024, raised for employers in 2025.

paragraphs.text: Employees pay 8% between £12,570 and £50,270 a year and 2% above; the main rate was 12% until January 2024 and 10% until April 2024. Employers pay 15% on earnings above £5,000 a year (£96 a week) since April 2025, up from 13.8% on earnings above £9,100.
National Insurance raises £204bn in 2025-26. Its share of GDP jumped from 5.8% to 6.7% this year, which the OBR attributes to the employer rise announced in October 2024.

The employer side is where the last two Budgets found money: the rate went from 13.8% to 15% and the threshold from £9,100 to £5,000 in April 2025, raising about £24bn a year. HMRC costs a further £2 a week off the threshold at about £0.45bn; employer contributions to pensions, on which no National Insurance is paid at all, are a relief worth £14.3bn a year.

briefings.title: Corporation tax
briefings.headline: 25% since 2023. Receipts hold at about 3.3% of GDP.

paragraphs.text: The main rate has been 25% since April 2023 (19% before), with a 19% small profits rate for profits under £50,000 and marginal relief to £250,000. Onshore corporation tax raises £96.8bn in 2025-26, 3.2% of GDP rising to 3.4% by 2030-31.

Reported for this Budget and uncosted: a business-rates surcharge on large warehouses and an online sales levy, both put off to the Budget when the pub rates cut was announced in July. Nobody has published a yield for either, so neither is on this desk; the business rates slider is the honest proxy.

briefings.title: VAT: one big rate and some very large exceptions
briefings.headline: One rate at 20%, and exceptions worth more than £60bn a year.

paragraphs.text: The standard rate has been 20% since 4 January 2011. VAT raises £181bn (5.9% of GDP) in 2025-26 and is forecast to reach £224bn in 2030-31 as spending shifts towards standard-rated goods.

The exceptions are large. HMRC's estimates of the cost of the reliefs in 2025-26: zero-rated food £27.4bn, new dwellings £14.6bn, the 5% rate on domestic fuel and power £7.0bn, domestic passenger transport £5.8bn, children's clothing £2.3bn and printed matter £1.7bn. HMRC warns that these estimates "do not represent the gain to the exchequer should a relief be abolished"; the toggles below show them as static costs.

briefings.title: Capital gains: small today, growing fast
briefings.headline: Capital gains receipts are up about 60% this year as sales were rushed ahead of the rate rise.

paragraphs.text: Capital gains tax: main rates 18% and 24% since 30 October 2024. Receipts are £21.8bn in 2025-26, about 60% up on the year because disposals were brought forward ahead of the rate rise, and are forecast to reach £34.9bn in 2030-31 on rising equity prices.

briefings.title: Wealth and property: inheritance tax, stamp duty and the surcharge
briefings.headline: Inheritance tax rises from £8.7bn to £14.7bn by 2030-31; stamp duty raises about twice that.

paragraphs.text: Inheritance tax: 40% on the part of an estate above the £325,000 nil-rate band, unchanged since 2009 and frozen to 2031. Receipts rise from £8.7bn in 2025-26 to £14.7bn in 2030-31 on rising asset prices, more estates above the threshold and the October 2024 changes to pensions and reliefs.

Stamp duty land tax on a main home: nothing to £125,000, 2% to £250,000, 5% to £925,000, 10% to £1.5 million and 12% above, with 5 percentage points on top for additional properties. Property transaction taxes raise £16.9bn in 2025-26, rising to £28.1bn in 2030-31.
Also reported: a flat 10% levy on every estate, reliefs and thresholds gone, to fund the National Care Service. The government says it has no plans; nobody has costed it, so it is not on this desk.

briefings.title: Duties: fuel, alcohol, tobacco, vehicles and flights
briefings.headline: Fuel duty has not risen since 2011-12; the smaller duties are where Chancellors usually look.

paragraphs.text: Fuel duty on petrol and diesel has been 52.95p a litre since the 5p cut of March 2022, and the OBR notes the rate has not been increased since 2011-12. Budget 2025 planned to unwind the cut in three stages (1p in September 2026, 2p in December 2026, 2p in March 2027) and to uprate with RPI from April 2027. Receipts are £24.2bn in 2025-26, peaking at about £27 billion in 2028-29 before electric vehicles erode the base.

Alcohol duty is charged per litre of pure alcohol by strength: from 1 February 2026, beer between 3.5% and 8.4% pays £22.58 a litre of alcohol and spirits above 22% pay £33.99. Alcohol duties raise £12.3bn in 2025-26.

The smaller duties are raised most Budgets. Vehicle excise duty is £200 a year for most cars after their first year; air passenger duty on an economy ticket is £8 within the UK and £15 to £106 abroad from April 2026, rising with inflation in 2027; cigarettes carry £353.50 per 1,000 plus 16.5% of the price since November 2025; and insurance premium tax has been 12% since 2017. HMRC publishes what a small change to each would raise.

briefings.title: Where the money goes
briefings.headline: Day-to-day budgets are set to 2028-29. After that there are only totals.

paragraphs.text: Day-to-day departmental spending (resource DEL) is £548bn in 2026-27 and grows at an average of 1.1% a year in real terms to £582bn in 2028-29, the last year of the Spending Review settlements. Capital budgets are £122bn in 2026-27, rising to £134bn by 2029-30.
The OBR projects the real per-person value of day-to-day spending to reach its highest level for two decades, excluding the pandemic peak.

After 2028-29 the Treasury has set totals, not departmental budgets: £594bn in 2029-30 and £614bn in 2030-31, implying 0.8% a year real growth. On the OBR's illustrative assumptions for the NHS, defence, aid and schools, 'unprotected' budgets would fall 4.4% a year in real terms in those two years; £13.5 billion more in 2030-31 would be needed to avoid that.

Welfare spending is £333bn in 2025-26, rising to £407bn in 2030-31; about half (£169bn this year) sits inside the welfare cap. The drivers are pensioner spending (larger cohorts and the triple lock) and health-related benefits, with disability caseloads forecast to rise from 6.5 million to 8.8 million by 2030-31.

facts.label: of which inside the welfare cap

briefings.title: What will be contested
briefings.headline: Health is protected. The Foreign Office, Transport and the Home Office are not.

paragraphs.text: Departmental cuts fall unevenly. The Spending Review protected health (NHS England up 3.0% a year in real terms to 2028-29) while the Foreign Office (down 6.9% a year), Transport (down 5.0%) and the Home Office (down 1.7%) take real cuts; anything you take from 'all other' budgets lands on departments already squeezed.

Changes to English departments reach the rest of the UK: under the Barnett formula the devolved governments' block grants move with comparable English spending, so a cut to health or education in England is also a cut in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The numbers here do not include those consequentials.

Your predecessor's welfare decisions were the reverse of savings: removing the two-child limit (£3.1bn in 2029-30), dropping the PIP eligibility changes (£4.5bn) and widening winter fuel payments (£1.3bn) all cost money, while £4.0bn of extra efficiency savings were pencilled in for departments.

briefings.title: Your predecessor's decisions
briefings.headline: Your predecessor's welfare U-turns cost about £9bn a year, and £4bn of efficiency savings are only pencilled in.

paragraphs.text: Budget 2025 removed the two-child limit in universal credit from April 2026 (costing £3.1bn in 2029-30), confirmed the PIP eligibility changes would not proceed (£4.5bn), paid winter fuel payments to pensioners with incomes up to £35,000 (£1.3bn) and counted £4.0bn of further efficiency savings from departments. Each can be reversed here at the Treasury's costing.

briefings.title: The Spending Review settlements
briefings.headline: Health, defence and schools are protected; the rest fall 4.4% a year in real terms after 2028-29.

paragraphs.text: The June 2025 Spending Review fixed day-to-day budgets to 2028-29. Average real growth a year from 2025-26: Health and Social Care 2.8% (NHS England 3.0%), Education 0.7%, Justice 1.8%, local government grant 1.1%, Defence 0.7%, Home Office -1.7%, Transport -5.0% and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office -6.9%. Total resource DEL excluding depreciation grows 1.2% a year.

The OBR’s forecast holds health, defence and schools to their settlements after 2028-29. The rest, just over a quarter of day-to-day spending, fall 4.4% a year in real terms; avoiding that would need spending £13.5 billion higher in 2030-31.

The OBR lists the pressures inside those settlements: special educational needs (a £6.3 billion pressure from 2028-29, partly met by £4.1 billion added to the envelope), defence (a straight-line path to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 would need about £6 billion more in 2028-29), asylum accommodation, public sector pay and £14 billion of efficiencies not being realised.
The levers below change each settlement by a percentage from April 2027 and carry 2029-30 and 2030-31 forward with the OBR's total path, an assumption shown in each drawer.

briefings.title: Public investment
briefings.headline: Investment adds to debt, not to the day-to-day budget the stability rule tests.

paragraphs.text: Capital DEL is £122bn in 2026-27 and £134bn in 2029-30 after the OBR's underspend assumptions (£9.7 billion this year, about £3.7 billion a year after). Defence capital rises from £23.2bn in 2025-26 to £33.2bn in 2029-30. Investment adds to borrowing and to net financial liabilities but not to the current budget, so it tests the investment rule, not the stability rule.

briefings.title: Working-age benefits
briefings.headline: Universal credit is £103bn in 2029-30, inside a cap the forecast already breaks.

paragraphs.text: In 2029-30 the OBR forecasts universal credit and legacy benefits of £103bn, child benefit £13.9bn and other welfare £24.3bn, all inside the welfare cap. Spending inside the cap is £199bn against a cap of £194.5 billion: above the cap but inside its 5% margin.

The think tanks pull both ways here: the Resolution Foundation and the Joseph Rowntree Foundation ask for housing support relinked to rents and a floor under deductions; the IFS shows a time limit on the new unemployment insurance saving money.

briefings.title: Pensioners and disability
briefings.headline: The state pension is outside the cap; disability benefits are inside it, and it is already breached.

paragraphs.text: In 2029-30 the OBR forecasts pensioner spending of £188bn (outside the welfare cap) and disability benefits of £61.1bn (inside it). Spending inside the cap is £199bn against a cap of £194.5 billion: above the cap but inside its 5% margin.

The OBR assumes incapacity caseload growth slows from 3.0% a year to about 1% by 2029-30 and calls that highly uncertain; it also notes that earlier eligibility reforms (disability living allowance to PIP) did not achieve the savings planned.

briefings.title: How the OBR will judge this Budget
briefings.headline: Headroom is a forecast. The OBR's typical five-year error is £33bn.

paragraphs.text: The OBR tests the stability rule on the current budget in the target year, the investment rule on whether net financial liabilities are falling as a share of GDP, and the welfare cap on capped spending against the cap and margin. It publishes its verdict with the Budget; the Chancellor may only suspend the rules in a significant shock, and the OBR judges whether one has occurred.

Headroom is a forecast, not a fact: the OBR's average absolute five-year forecast difference for receipts is 0.9% of GDP, about £33 billion by 2030-31. A Budget that passes by a few billion is one revision away from failing.

briefings.title: Your assumptions are not the OBR's
briefings.headline: These are your assumptions, not the OBR's. It publishes its own on 28 October.

paragraphs.text: Any change you made to the interest rate, growth or inflation sliders is your view, costed with the OBR's published sensitivities. On 28 October the OBR will publish its own updated forecast; the arithmetic here shows what your Budget looks like if your assumptions turn out to be right.

briefings.title: The Prime Minister's schemes
briefings.headline: These are the Prime Minister's schemes. Nobody has certified their cost; each card shows our arithmetic.

paragraphs.text: Everywhere else on this screen the baseline is a Spending Review settlement or an OBR line. These programmes are not government policy yet, so nobody has certified a costing. Each card states the method, the published figures it rests on and what it assumes, and wears the assumption badge for it. Open one and you can check the arithmetic.

Two kinds of money sit side by side here. Capital grants for homes score in the capital budget and test the investment rule; a free lunch, a bus cap or a retraining programme is day-to-day spending and tests the stability rule. The Charter treats them differently, and so does your headroom.

briefings.title: Ways to deliver
briefings.headline: Each priority comes with a few costed ways to deliver it. Every option is a lever the game already prices.

paragraphs.text: The options here are the settlements, programmes and welfare lines the game already carries: a department's day-to-day budget moved against its Spending Review path, a programme the government has costed, or a reform a think tank has costed and badged as such. Each card shows the engine's figure for the target year and the minister's own line on what the money buys, and what it does not.

briefings.title: Ways to afford it
briefings.headline: The gap is your target minus the headroom you have left. Every way to close it says who pays.

paragraphs.text: HMRC's ready reckoner costs the rate and threshold changes and the Treasury's scorecards cost the decisions of the last two Budgets; where only a think tank has costed a measure, the card wears the assumption badge and, where the measure needs its own Act or is collected late, an earliest start. The manifesto's tax lock fences off income tax rates, National Insurance and VAT: an option that crosses it says so before you choose it.
